issue:
Table column collapsed to width 0 (header dropped, cells blank) when sibling has long unbreakable tokens

**Describe the bug**

When a markdown table has one column containing long unbreakable tokens (e.g. snake_case identifiers), and another short column whose header is wider than its cells, glow's table renderer allocates near-zero width to the short column under tight width budgets. The header label disappears entirely (not even truncated to `…`) and every cell in that column renders blank, even though the cell content (a single character) would fit.

This makes data invisible — readers see the table and have no indication that an entire column exists.

**Setup**
- glow version v2.1.1
- OS: Fedora 44 (Linux 6.19.14)
- Shell: zsh
- Locale: en_US.UTF-8

**To Reproduce**

`repro.md`:

```markdown
| Feature | Status | identifier | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| feature one with a moderately long name | Y | module_alpha::test_long_identifier_name_first | comment one. Some explanatory text describing behavior here. |
| feature two with another moderately long name | Y | module_alpha::test_long_identifier_name_second | comment two. More explanatory text describing behavior here. |
```

Run `glow -s notty -w 80 repro.md`:

```
   Feature               | | identifier            | Notes
  -----------------------|-|-----------------------|------------------------
   feature one with a    | | module_alpha::test_lo | comment one. Some
   moderately long name  | | ng_identifier_name_fi | explanatory text
                         | | rst                   | describing behavior
                         | |                       | here.
   feature two with      | | module_alpha::test_lo | comment two. More
   another moderately    | | ng_identifier_name_se | explanatory text
   long name             | | cond                  | describing behavior
                         | |                       | here.
```

Notice the second column header is empty (where `Status` should be), and every `Y` cell is blank. The column has been allocated only 1 cell of width — not enough for the header label or even a single-character cell value. This is plain ASCII content, so it's not a rune-width issue.

**Expected behavior**

The Status column should never shrink below `max(len(header), max_content_width)`. At `-w 80` the column should be at least 6 chars wide ("Status") with `Y` rendered. If the total budget cannot accommodate every column at its minimum, glow should either truncate the wide column with `…` or flow content to additional lines — not silently erase a column.

**Width sensitivity**

Same input, varying width:

| `-w` | Status column |
| --- | --- |
| 78 | collapsed (header missing, cells blank) |
| 80 | collapsed (header missing, cells blank) |
| 100 | renders correctly: `Status` + `Y` |
| 120 | renders correctly |

So the bug only manifests under tight budgets, and there is no flag/config to force a per-column minimum.

**Likely location**

Bug is in glamour's table column-width distribution (probably `glamour/ansi/table.go` interacting with `lipgloss/table`'s width allocation), not in glow itself. Distinct from:
- glamour#486 (different root cause: `indent*margin` vs `indent+margin` math)
- glamour#344, #402 (max-col-width / wrap toggle features)
- lipgloss#493 (missing ellipsis when wrap disabled)

issue:
Authentication Rate Limit Bypass via X-Forwarded-For Spoofing

### Description

reported privately on 22 May 2026 - no response since: https://github.com/glanceapp/glance/security/advisories/GHSA-427g-2pm7-r356



### Summary

When the `proxied` server option is set to `true` (as recommended in the documentation for reverse proxy deployments), an attacker can bypass the login rate limit entirely by spoofing the `X-Forwarded-For` header. This removes the brute-force protection on the login endpoint, allowing unlimited password guesses.

### Details

Glance enforces a rate limit of 5 failed login attempts per 5-minute window per IP address. The IP address used for this check is resolved in `addressOfRequest` (`internal/glance/glance.go`, lines 369-396):

```go
func (a *application) addressOfRequest(r *http.Request) string {
    // ...
    if !a.Config.Server.Proxied {
        return remoteAddrWithoutPort()
    }

    forwardedFor := r.Header.Get("X-Forwarded-For")
    if forwardedFor == "" {
        return remoteAddrWithoutPort()
    }

    ips := strings.Split(forwardedFor, ",")
    if len(ips) == 0 || ips[0] == "" {
        return remoteAddrWithoutPort()
    }

    return ips[0]
}
```

When `Proxied: true`, the function returns `ips[0]` -- the first (leftmost) value in the `X-Forwarded-For` header. This value is supplied by the client and can be set to any arbitrary string. A standard nginx reverse proxy using `$proxy_add_x_forwarded_for` appends the real client IP but preserves any client-supplied prefix, meaning a request with `X-Forwarded-For: 1.2.3.4` arrives at Glance as `X-Forwarded-For: 1.2.3.4, <real_ip>`, and `ips[0]` resolves to the attacker-chosen value.

The official documentation at `docs/configuration.md` lines 269-273 explicitly instructs users behind nginx, Traefik, NPM, or any other reverse proxy to set `proxied: true`:

> In order for this feature to work correctly, Glance must know the real IP address of requests. If you're using a reverse proxy such as nginx, Traefik, NPM, etc, you must set the `proxied` property in the `server` configuration to `true`.

This means the documented deployment path for production instances is precisely the configuration under which rate limiting is defeatable.

The `handleAuthenticationAttempt` function (`internal/glance/auth.go`, lines 134-248) calls `a.addressOfRequest(r)` at line 142 and uses the returned IP as the key into `a.failedAuthAttempts`. By rotating the spoofed IP value on each request, an attacker sees a fresh attempt counter for every login try.

### PoC

Prerequisites: Glance deployed behind a reverse proxy with `proxied: true` in `glance.yml`.

The following shell loop bypasses rate limiting by rotating a spoofed source IP on each request:

```bash
TARGET="http://glance.example.com"
USERNAME="admin"
WORDLIST="passwords.txt"

i=1
while IFS= read -r password; do
  curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code} $password\n" \
    -X POST "$TARGET/api/authenticate" \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -H "X-Forwarded-For: 10.0.0.$((i % 254 + 1))" \
    -d "{\"username\":\"$USERNAME\",\"password\":\"$password\"}"
  i=$((i + 1))
done < "$WORDLIST"
```

Each request presents a unique IP to Glance's rate limiter. The rate limit is never triggered regardless of how many attempts are made.

### Impact

Any attacker who can reach the Glance login endpoint can perform unlimited password guessing against any account. The effectiveness depends on the strength of the target password. Accounts with weak or common passwords are fully compromised. Successful authentication grants full access to the Glance dashboard, including any widgets that expose sensitive data (API keys in custom-api widgets, Docker container details, internal service URLs, etc.).

Deployments are most exposed when the login page is publicly reachable (e.g., VPS exposed to the internet), which is the common self-hosted scenario described in the documentation.

RPC clients can discover services inside Kubernetes by using the `k8s` target
scheme:

```go
c := zrpc.RpcClientConf{
    NonBlock: true,
    Target:   "k8s://dev/demo-rpc:8080",
}
```

EndpointSlices, so the service account used by the client must be allowed to
read EndpointSlices in the target namespace:

rules:
  - apiGroups: ["discovery.k8s.io"]

Bug:filex.LastLine returns a wrong line when the content after the last separator is a multiple of 1024 bytes

`filex.LastLine` returns a wrong line when the content after the last separator is a multiple of 1024 bytes

## Description

`filex.LastLine` can return a wrong result: part (or all) of the **previous** line gets merged into the returned "last line".

The bug is triggered when the number of bytes **after the last separator `'\n'`** is an exact multiple of the internal block size (`bufSize = 1024`) — for example when the last line is exactly 1024 bytes long and the file does not end with a newline. Fixed-length record files and machine-generated logs can hit this alignment.

## Root cause

In `core/filex/file.go`, `lastLine()` reads the file backwards in 1024-byte blocks. Before scanning a block for `'\n'`, it unconditionally trims a trailing newline:

```go
if buf[n-1] == '\n' {
	buf = buf[:n-1]
	n--
} else {
	buf = buf[:n]
}
```

This trim is only correct for the **tail block** (the first block read), where a trailing `'\n'` is the file's final newline.

For an **interior block**, a `'\n'` at the block's last byte is the **start boundary of the last line** (the next block, already read, begins exactly at the start of the last line). Trimming it destroys that boundary; the remaining block then contains no `'\n'`, so the whole block — which belongs to the *previous* line — is prepended to the accumulated result:

```go
last = append(buf, last...)   // buf belongs to the previous line, wrongly merged
```

Precise trigger condition: `(fileSize - lastSeparatorOffset - 1) % 1024 == 0`, i.e. the length of the content after the last `'\n'` is a multiple of 1024.

## Reproduction

```go
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"os"
	"path/filepath"
	"strings"

	"github.com/zeromicro/go-zero/core/filex"
)

func main() {
	// any previous line + '\n' + a last line of exactly 1024 bytes, no trailing newline
	content := "previous line\n" + strings.Repeat("C", 1024)

	dir, _ := os.MkdirTemp("", "repro")
	defer os.RemoveAll(dir)
	f := filepath.Join(dir, "t.txt")
	os.WriteFile(f, []byte(content), 0o644)

	got, _ := filex.LastLine(f)
	fmt.Printf("expected len=1024, got len=%d, got=%q...\n", len(got), got[:min(24, len(got))])
}
```

Output:

```
expected len=1024, got len=1037, got="previous lineCCCCCCCCCCCC"...
```

The previous line (13 bytes) is merged into the result. Adding just one byte to the last line (1025 bytes) makes the bug disappear, which confirms the alignment condition.

## Suggested fix

Only trim the trailing newline on the block that reaches the end of the file:

```go
// only the tail block can end with the file's final newline;
// an interior block's trailing '\n' is the start boundary of the last line
if offset+bufLen == info.Size() && buf[n-1] == '\n' {
	buf = buf[:n-1]
	n--
} else {
	buf = buf[:n]
}
```

With this change, an interior block ending in `'\n'` is handled correctly by the existing backward scan: it finds the `'\n'` at `i = n-1` and returns `buf[n:] + last`, which is exactly the accumulated `last` (the last line starts at the next block).

## Environment

- go-zero: master (`core/filex/file.go`)
- go version go1.27.1 darwin/arm64

Bug: filex.SplitLineChunks returns EOF error when the last line is longer than the preferred chunk size

Bug: `filex.SplitLineChunks` returns `EOF` error when the last line is longer than the preferred chunk size

## Description

`filex.SplitLineChunks` returns an unexpected `EOF` error for a **perfectly valid file** when the last line is longer than `preferSize` (i.e. the ideal cut point falls inside the final line).

Related: found while investigating #5787 (another edge case in `core/filex`).

## Reproduction

```go
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"os"
	"path/filepath"
	"strings"

	"github.com/zeromicro/go-zero/core/filex"
)

func main() {
	// last line (3000 bytes) is longer than preferSize
	content := "a\n" + strings.Repeat("b", 3000)

	dir, _ := os.MkdirTemp("", "repro")
	defer os.RemoveAll(dir)
	f := filepath.Join(dir, "t.txt")
	os.WriteFile(f, []byte(content), 0o644)

	ranges, err := filex.SplitLineChunks(f, 2)
	fmt.Printf("ranges=%v, err=%v\n", ranges, err)
}
```

Output:

```
ranges=[], err=EOF
```

Expected: no error, and since the last line must not be split across chunks (documented guarantee "The whole line are guaranteed to be split in the same chunk"), one chunk `[0, 3002)` covering the whole file.

## Root cause

`SplitLineChunks` estimates each chunk's ideal stop as `offset + preferSize` and then calls `nextRange` → `skipPartialLine` to push the stop forward to the start of the next line.

`skipPartialLine` implicitly assumes there is always a next line after the cut point. When the cut point falls **inside the last line**, there is no next line: it scans forward to EOF without finding a `'\n'`, and returns `io.EOF`:

```go
if n == 0 {
    return 0, io.EOF
}
```

`nextRange` and `SplitLineChunks` then propagate this as an error:

```go
offsetRange, err := nextRange(file, offset, offset+preferSize)
if err != nil {
    return nil, err   // io.EOF leaks to the caller
}
```

Trigger condition: `offset + preferSize < fileSize` (so the top-of-loop tail check doesn't fire) **and** there is no `'\n'` in `[offset+preferSize, fileSize)` — i.e. the ideal cut point lands inside the final line. Note the tail check `offset+preferSize >= info.Size()` only protects the final short tail; it cannot protect a long last line.

## Suggested fix

Special-case `io.EOF` in `SplitLineChunks`: it precisely means "the cut point is inside the last line", so merge the last line entirely into the current chunk with `Stop = info.Size()`:

```go
offsetRange, err := nextRange(file, offset, offset+preferSize)
if errors.Is(err, io.EOF) {
    // cut point is inside the last line; keep the line whole
    offsetRange = OffsetRange{
        File:  filename,
        Start: offset,
        Stop:  info.Size(),
    }
} else if err != nil {
    return nil, err
}
```

The existing `if offsetRange.Stop < info.Size()` check then exits the loop naturally (no empty trailing chunk).

Verified with: normal multi-line files (unchanged output), cut point landing on trailing newlines (unchanged), cut point inside last line at offset 0 and mid-file (previously `EOF` error, now a single whole-file/whole-line chunk).

## Environment

- go-zero: master (`core/filex/lookup.go`)
- go version go1.27.1 darwin/arm64

issue:
value_chain swallows a TypeError raised while iterating an argument

`value_chain` treats a `TypeError` raised *while consuming* an argument as evidence that the argument is not iterable. The exception is swallowed, and the partially-consumed object is emitted into the output stream after the items it already produced.

### Reproduction

```python
>>> from more_itertools import value_chain
>>> list(value_chain(map(len, ['ab', 'cde', 5])))
[2, 3, <map object at 0x104c6e530>]
```

The `TypeError: object of type 'int' has no len()` never reaches the caller. The trailing item is the exhausted `map` object itself, so it carries no data:

```python
>>> out = list(value_chain(map(len, ['ab', 'cde', 5])))
>>> list(out[-1])
[]
```

`itertools.chain` and more-itertools' own `always_iterable` both propagate on the same input:

```python
>>> list(chain(map(len, ['ab', 'cde', 5])))
TypeError: object of type 'int' has no len()
>>> list(always_iterable(map(len, ['ab', 'cde', 5])))
TypeError: object of type 'int' has no len()
```

Any lazy argument can trigger this — a generator, a `map`, a file-backed iterator — so a genuine bug in caller code is reported as a stray object in the output rather than as an exception.

### Cause

[`more.py` L4416](https://github.com/more-itertools/more-itertools/blob/bc8be10/more_itertools/more.py#L4416):

```python
        try:
            yield from value
        except TypeError:
            yield value
```

`yield from` consumes lazily, so the guard stays active for the entire consumption of `value` instead of only classifying it. The `except` branch is meant to catch the classification failure — an object that cannot be iterated — but it also catches every `TypeError` produced downstream while iterating.

Present since `8dbf8ae` (2020-12-01), the commit that added `value_chain`. Reproduces on released 11.1.0.

### Suggested fix

Classify with `iter()`, then consume outside the guard:

```python
        try:
            it = iter(value)
        except TypeError:
            yield value
        else:
            yield from it
```

This is what the sibling `always_iterable` already does. Objects that cannot be iterated at all — including those whose `__iter__` raises `TypeError` — are still emitted as-is, so the documented behaviour is unchanged.

I have a branch with this fix and regression tests ready and will open a PR against this issue.

numeric_range: len(), `in` and index() disagree with the items produced, for float steps

`numeric_range` derives `len()`, `__contains__` and `index()` by dividing by the step, but produces its items by repeated multiplication. With floats the two disagree, so a range can report a length that does not match what it yields, and can deny membership to its own items.

On 11.1.0 and on current master (`2fe1b2e`):

### `len()` disagrees with iteration, in both directions

```pycon
>>> from more_itertools import numeric_range

>>> r = numeric_range(-8.732, -13.532, -2.4)
>>> list(r)
[-8.732, -11.132]
>>> len(r)
3
>>> r[2]                      # counted, but it is the excluded stop value
-13.532

>>> r = numeric_range(-69.37276490678778, -29.8339073344664, 4.942357196540172)
>>> len(list(r))
9
>>> len(r)
8
>>> r[8]                      # an item iteration yields, but indexing cannot reach
IndexError: numeric range object index out of range
```

### Items are not `in` their own range

```pycon
>>> r = numeric_range(0.0, 1.0, 0.1)
>>> r[3]
0.30000000000000004
>>> r[3] in r
False
>>> r.index(r[3])
ValueError: 0.30000000000000004 is not in numeric range
>>> sum(1 for v in r if v not in r)
5
```

`count()` follows `__contains__`, so it returns 0 for those items too.

### Cause

`__iter__` and `_get_by_index` compute items as `start + n * step`. Membership and length instead reason about the step arithmetically:

- `__contains__` and `index` test `(value - start) % step == 0`. `0.30000000000000004` is what the range yields at index 3, but it is not an exact multiple of `0.1`, so the remainder is not zero.
- `_len` computes `divmod(distance, step)` and rounds up. That measures the distance to cover rather than counting the items actually produced, and lands one over or one under when the multiplication does not agree with the division.

Exact types are unaffected — `Decimal`, `Fraction`, `int`, and `datetime`/`timedelta` all give a zero remainder for their own items, so they behave the same before and after. This is specific to binary floats.

The `__contains__` shortcut dates to #363 (2020); `_len` has had the same shape since it was introduced.

### Note

This is not only about surprising float repr, which the docstring already warns about. `numeric_range` is a `Sequence`, and here `r[i] not in r` and `len(r) != len(list(r))` — the object disagrees with itself, so `.index()`, `.count()`, `in`, `len()` and indexing give inconsistent answers for the same range.

I have a fix that settles all four against the items the range actually produces, keeping the exact-type behavior and the current performance for them. Happy to open a PR if you would like it.

**Describe the bug**
Prior to #3547, mathjs could parse conditional expressions in which the true-expr happened to be a floating-point number beginning with a decimal point. Now such expressions may throw an error.

`math.evaluate('true?.3:.7')` -- throws "SyntaxError: Unexpected operator ?. (char 7)". It previously returned the number `.3`.

The error is occurring because `parseConditional` first attempts to `parseLogicalOr`, as that element might be the condition-expr of a conditional. In that attempt, `parseLogicalOr` eventually descends down to `parseSymbol`, which succeeds on `true` (producing a ConstantNode of the boolean true value), and then it attempts to parse any accessors to that symbol, at which point it eagerly consumes the `?.` as an optional chaining operator, not realizing it could also be the start of a conditional followed by a true-expr that happens to begin with a dot, and the parse fails when the next token (`3`) is not anything that can currently legally follow the optional chaining operator.

It isn't enough just to save state and unwind to just before the `?.` was read and return whatever was parsed before the `?.` was encountered, since then it will just continue to be tokenized as `?.` and parseConditional won't see the `?` token it needs to begin a conditional.

So that would suggest that to fix this regression, `?.` needs to be removed as a delimiter, so that it will always be parsed as just a `?` token, and then parseAccessors has to deal with looking at the `?` token and then checking for a `.` after that, and possibly revert to the state before the `?` was examined if no parse as optional chaining is forthcoming.

variable named E blocks .-operators

**Describe the bug**
If a variable happens to be named `E`, then you cannot implicitly multiply it by a constant and then apply an operator that starts with `.` unless you insert whitespace.

**To Reproduce**
```
const eval = math.evaluate
const scope = {E: [1, 2]}
eval('3E', scope)  // [3, 6]
eval('E.*2', scope)  // [2, 4]
eval('3E.*2', scope)  // SyntaxError: Digit expected, got "." (char 2)
eval('3E .*2', scope)  // [6, 12]
```

**Discussion**
I understand that we don't want fractional exponential notation e.g. `3E.7` but there does not seem to be any reason to disallow  a bona fide operator that happens to start with `.` after an expression that happens to end in `E` or `e`.

I use nunjucks to power an internal tool at my work which allows users to configure nunjucks templates as part of a process automation tool.
